Launch page — revised messaging package, version 7 (for review; not published)

Purpose and status
This is a review-only draft for the relaunch. It is not published, sent, or treated as evidence of improved performance.

Evidence base
- Internal launch context: the goal is to convert one-person-company founders; the current signal is low signup conversion and visitors do not recognise themselves (company record: launch/context; application observation ev_1790031112914_8retyw).
- The available internal launch context does not establish which specific copy variant will perform better. Improvement therefore requires a controlled comparison before publication.

Current message retained for comparison
Headline: “Somebody: an AI manager for your business.”
Subhead: “Automate your workflows with AI.”
Status: launch not converting; visitors leave without signing up.
Assumed audience: generic “businesses”.
Assumed pain point: “too many tools”.

Launch messaging diagnosis
Symptoms (observed outcomes, not root causes)
- Low signup conversion.
- Visitors leave without signing up.
- Visitors do not recognise themselves.
- The message is experienced as broad/tool-like rather than immediately relevant.

Working diagnosis
The current message does not explicitly identify one-person-company founders or connect the product to the day-to-day burden of running a lean business. This is a working hypothesis for testing, not an established causal finding.

Revised audience, problem and outcome
- Primary audience: one-person-company founders and lean-SME operators.
- Problem framing: the founder is carrying recurring business work across too many disconnected workflows and must keep the business moving while doing the work themselves.
- Desired outcome: a clearer, more relevant entry point to Somebody as an AI manager that helps coordinate business workflows, subject to product-claim review.

Revised launch-page copy
Headline: “Run your one-person company with an AI manager.”
Subhead: “Somebody helps you keep the work moving across your business, so you can spend less time coordinating tasks and more time doing the work that matters.”
Primary CTA: “See how Somebody can help”
Supporting copy: “Built for founders who are the operator, project manager, and decision-maker in one.”
Proof/claim guardrail: Do not add specific automation, integration, time-saved, performance, customer, or outcome claims unless product evidence and approval support them.

Short-form launch copy
Version A — direct audience identification
“You run the business and the business runs through you. Somebody is an AI manager for one-person companies and lean teams. See how it can help keep your work moving.”

Version B — current control
“Somebody: an AI manager for your business. Automate your workflows with AI.”

Launch-surface guidance
- Landing page: use the revised headline, subhead, supporting copy, and primary CTA above; retain Version B as the control in the comparison.
- Short-form launch surfaces: use Version A without adding unsupported product or performance claims.
- All surfaces: keep the audience label consistent—one-person-company founders and lean-SME operators—and link the CTA to the same signup path.
- Review-only: do not publish, send, or represent the revised copy as validated until the acceptance criteria below are met.

Acceptance criteria
1. Completeness: the review draft contains audience, problem, desired outcome, landing-page copy, short-form copy, surface guidance, comparison design, decision rule, assumptions, risks, and approval status.
2. Internal consistency: every launch surface identifies the same primary audience and uses the same product framing; no surface uses the generic audience framing as the revised treatment.
3. Claim safety: product/legal review flags zero unsupported specific claims before publication; unresolved flags block publication.
4. Experiment setup: before publication, pre-register the audience definition, allocation method, exposure window, signup-conversion event, and decision rule for the revised treatment versus the retained control.
5. Primary outcome: measure signup conversion as signups divided by eligible unique visitors for each variant over the pre-registered exposure window.
6. Decision rule: publish the revised treatment only if it meets the pre-registered comparison rule and has no unresolved claim or implementation issues; otherwise retain the control or revise and test again. The numeric threshold and required sample size remain to be set by the launch owner before the comparison begins; they must not be inferred from the current evidence.
7. Instrumentation: verify that variant assignment, eligible visitors, CTA clicks, and completed signups are recorded consistently before the test starts.
8. Review status: obtain explicit product-claim and audience-fit review, then record the experiment plan and result separately from this draft.

Material assumptions
- One-person-company founders and lean-SME operators are the intended launch audience, based on the internal launch context.
- Explicit audience identification will improve recognition and may improve signup conversion; this is a hypothesis, not evidence of impact.
- The stated product framing is accurate enough for review; exact capabilities and claims still require product-claim review.
- The signup path and analytics can distinguish eligible visitors and variants without introducing material measurement bias.

Material risks and mitigations
- Risk: “AI manager” or “keep the work moving” may overstate capabilities. Mitigation: product-claim review; block publication for unresolved issues.
- Risk: the audience or problem hypothesis may be wrong. Mitigation: controlled comparison and review of audience-fit feedback.
- Risk: insufficient or inconsistent traffic/measurement may make results inconclusive. Mitigation: pre-register the exposure window, sample-size requirement, metric, and decision rule before running the comparison.
- Risk: inconsistent copy across surfaces could dilute the test. Mitigation: use the surface guidance and one shared signup path.
- Risk: the current evidence does not establish a winning variant. Mitigation: treat this as review-only and do not claim improvement before measurement.

Next review actions
- Confirm product-claim accuracy and audience fit.
- Pre-register the comparison audience, exposure window, signup-conversion metric, sample-size requirement, and numeric decision rule.
- Verify instrumentation.
- Run an approved controlled comparison before publishing.

Status: for review only; not published or sent.

- Internal launch context: the goal is to convert one-person-company founders; the current signal is low signup conversion and visitors do not recognise themselves (company record: launch/context).
- Founder-language research: founders describe switching between selling, researching, following up, and doing the work; “AI manager” can sound like a dashboard or advisor; concrete outcome ownership and finished work are clearer than generic workflow automation (verified acquisition: sim_result_a4505571e05d92f81d9cffef).

Symptoms (observed outcomes, not root causes)
- Low signup conversion.
- Visitors leave without signing up.
- Visitors do not recognise themselves.
- The message is experienced as broad/tool-like rather than immediately relevant.

Prioritized principal causes
1. Audience is too generic — HIGH likely impact / HIGH confidence.
   The headline says “for your business” while the launch goal is specifically one-person-company founders. This weakens self-recognition and relevance. Evidence: launch/context; current page copy above.
2. The promise is framed as a category or mechanism instead of an accountable outcome — HIGH likely impact / MEDIUM-high confidence.
   “AI manager” and “automate your workflows” do not make clear that work is carried through to a finished result; the founder-language evidence says these phrases can read as a dashboard, advisor, or broad tool. Evidence: sim_result_a4505571e05d92f81d9cffef.
3. The pain point is misidentified or underspecified — HIGH likely impact / MEDIUM confidence.
   The page assumes “too many tools,” while the observed founder language points to fragmented attention and switching between selling, research, follow-up, and delivery. This likely prevents the visitor from seeing their actual problem in the copy. Evidence: current page assumption above; sim_result_a4505571e05d92f81d9cffef.
4. Differentiation is not explicit — MEDIUM likely impact / MEDIUM confidence.
   The current copy does not explain the distinctive make-versus-buy capability: noticing missing capability, getting what is needed, doing the work, and returning with a finished result. This leaves the product sounding like generic automation. Evidence: sim_result_a4505571e05d92f81d9cffef.

Recommended message direction
Lead with the one-person-company founder’s outcome and accountability, name the fragmented-work problem, and then explain the capability underneath. Candidate direction (for review):
Headline: “Stop switching between every job in your company.”
Subhead: “Somebody is the accountable AI manager for one-person companies—when work needs a capability you don’t have, it gets what’s needed, does the work, and comes back with a finished result.”

Confidence note
Confidence is based on one internal launch record plus one verified founder-language acquisition; impact rankings are hypotheses, not causal proof. Validate with message testing and signup-conversion measurement before treating the ranking as conclusive.

Revised launch-page package — version 4

Primary audience
One-person-company founders and lean SMEs who switch between selling, researching, following up, and delivering the work themselves.

Headline
"Run your business with an AI manager that gets the work done."

Subhead

Intended launch surface

Internal consistency checks
- Audience is consistently described as one-person-company founders and lean SMEs.
- The message uses the same product framing throughout: an AI manager that helps move work forward and finish it.

1. Self-recognition: In a review survey of qualified one-person-company founders and lean-SME visitors, at least 70% should identify the page as relevant to them, measured by the agreed “relevant to me” response.

Measurement plan

- Measure self-recognition, message comprehension, and visitor-to-signup conversion.
- Segment results for one-person-company founders and lean SMEs where identifiable.

Launch messaging diagnosis
Symptoms (observed outcomes, not root causes)
- Low signup conversion.
- Visitors leave without signing up.
- Visitors do not recognise themselves.
- The message is experienced as broad/tool-like rather than immediately relevant.

Working diagnosis
The current message does not explicitly identify one-person-company founders or connect the product to the day-to-day burden of running a lean business. This is a working hypothesis for testing, not an established causal finding.

Revised audience, problem and outcome
- Primary audience: one-person-company founders and lean-SME operators.
- Problem framing: the founder is carrying recurring business work across too many disconnected workflows and must keep the business moving while doing the work themselves.
- Desired outcome: a clearer, more relevant entry point to Somebody as an AI manager that helps coordinate business workflows, subject to product-claim review.

Revised launch-page copy
Headline: “Run your one-person company with an AI manager.”
Subhead: “Somebody helps you keep the work moving across your business, so you can spend less time coordinating tasks and more time doing the work that matters.”
Primary CTA: “See how Somebody can help”
Supporting copy: “Built for founders who are the operator, project manager, and decision-maker in one.”
Proof/claim guardrail: Do not add specific automation, integration, time-saved, performance, customer, or outcome claims unless product evidence and approval support them.

Short-form launch copy
Version A — direct audience identification
“You run the business and the business runs through you. Somebody is an AI manager for one-person companies and lean teams. See how it can help keep your work moving.”

Version B — current control
“Somebody: an AI manager for your business. Automate your workflows with AI.”

Launch-surface guidance
- Landing page: use the revised headline, subhead, supporting copy, and primary CTA above; retain Version B as the control in the comparison.
- Short-form launch surfaces: use Version A without adding unsupported product or performance claims.
- All surfaces: keep the audience label consistent—one-person-company founders and lean-SME operators—and link the CTA to the same signup path.
- Review-only: do not publish, send, or represent the revised copy as validated until the acceptance criteria below are met.

Acceptance criteria
1. Completeness: the review draft contains audience, problem, desired outcome, landing-page copy, short-form copy, surface guidance, comparison design, decision rule, assumptions, risks, and approval status.
2. Internal consistency: every launch surface identifies the same primary audience and uses the same product framing; no surface uses the generic audience framing as the revised treatment.
3. Claim safety: product/legal review flags zero unsupported specific claims before publication; unresolved flags block publication.
4. Experiment setup: before publication, pre-register the audience definition, allocation method, exposure window, signup-conversion event, and decision rule for the revised treatment versus the retained control.
5. Primary outcome: measure signup conversion as signups divided by eligible unique visitors for each variant over the pre-registered exposure window.
6. Decision rule: publish the revised treatment only if it meets the pre-registered comparison rule and has no unresolved claim or implementation issues; otherwise retain the control or revise and test again. The numeric threshold and required sample size remain to be set by the launch owner before the comparison begins; they must not be inferred from the current evidence.
7. Instrumentation: verify that variant assignment, eligible visitors, CTA clicks, and completed signups are recorded consistently before the test starts.
8. Review status: obtain explicit product-claim and audience-fit review, then record the experiment plan and result separately from this draft.

Material assumptions
- One-person-company founders and lean-SME operators are the intended launch audience, based on the internal launch context.
- Explicit audience identification will improve recognition and may improve signup conversion; this is a hypothesis, not evidence of impact.
- The stated product framing is accurate enough for review; exact capabilities and claims still require product-claim review.
- The signup path and analytics can distinguish eligible visitors and variants without introducing material measurement bias.

Material risks and mitigations
- Risk: “AI manager” or “keep the work moving” may overstate capabilities. Mitigation: product-claim review; block publication for unresolved issues.
- Risk: the audience or problem hypothesis may be wrong. Mitigation: controlled comparison and review of audience-fit feedback.
- Risk: insufficient or inconsistent traffic/measurement may make results inconclusive. Mitigation: pre-register the exposure window, sample-size requirement, metric, and decision rule before running the comparison.
- Risk: inconsistent copy across surfaces could dilute the test. Mitigation: use the surface guidance and one shared signup path.
- Risk: the current evidence does not establish a winning variant. Mitigation: treat this as review-only and do not claim improvement before measurement.

Next review actions
- Confirm product-claim accuracy and audience fit.
- Pre-register the comparison audience, exposure window, signup-conversion metric, sample-size requirement, and numeric decision rule.
- Verify instrumentation.
- Run an approved controlled comparison before publishing.
